title: Content Beyond Readability
intro: A readability score says text is easy to read, not easy to use. Three layers sit above it.

learn.title: Four layers of usable content
learn.text:
**Readability** — plain words, short sentences. Necessary, not sufficient.
**Structure** — headings, chunks, lists, links, so people can scan and jump.
**Information architecture** — content organised by users' mental models and tasks.
**Voice and tone** — consistent personality; tone adapts to the moment.

Wikipedia is his example: dense subject matter made navigable through structure and linking.

try.q: Dense technical content scores poorly on readability but users find what they need. What's carrying it?
try.explain: Wikipedia is the example: hard subject matter made navigable.

learn.title: Front-load and group by task
learn.text:
**Front-load the point** and let headings carry the scan.

**Group content the way users look for it** — use card sorts and tree tests, not the org chart.

**Match terms to users' words**, which is the shared-meaning idea from conversational UX.

try.q: Which methods should decide how content is grouped?

learn.title: Using LLMs for content audits
learn.text:
LLM audits are useful **for scale** — word counts, tone checks, readability across hundreds of pages — but judge the results yourself.

*Context: written in 2023 around a ChatGPT-4 audit, so the prompt workflow has dated. Some statistics the original cites (such as a “124% more likely to engage” figure attributed to NN/g) can't be found in the named sources — keep the principles, not the numbers.*

try.q: What are LLM content audits good for?
options: Judging whether the tone is right
try.explain: Use them for breadth, then apply your own judgement.

test.q: What does a readability score tell you?
options: That the text is easy to read
That the page is easy to use
Repeat the key phrase for SEO
test.explain: Front-load the point and let headings do the navigating.

test.q: Which layer is about matching users' mental models?
test.explain: Organised the way users look for things.

test.q: What is the difference between voice and tone?
options: Voice is constant; tone adapts to the moment
Voice is written; tone is spoken
Voice is the brand's; tone is the writer's

test.q: Why treat the article's statistics with caution?
options: Some can't be traced to the sources named
They come from a single industry
They were measured on desktop only
test.explain: The principles hold; the numbers don't check out.
